name: Double-stud L-track cargo-anchor engagement
equipment: US Cargo Control1519-DSR pear-link double-stud fitting with its compatible full-size logistic rail. Do not combine Ancra50362-11 dimensions with this product.
importance: Impact on jobs. Securing/inspecting cargo is regular core driver work, according to the recovered primary-source summary. Historical2025 claim2,221,200 drivers; source must be re-read before treating this as verified here. Exact fitting use by all drivers is not claimed.
comparators: T-nut insertion, quarter-turn and sliding under profile lips. Same undercut capture and positioning; entry direction alone failed novelty in#939.
DIN hook/pivot/spring-latch mounting. Same retained rail-mounted endpoint; hook topology differs from simultaneous two-disc capture.
Bayonet axial push/rotation under a roof. Same lug capture; L-track translates and independently prevents reverse travel rather than locking by rotational stop.
distinction: Potentially distinct simultaneous two-stud aperture registration, under-lip translation and independent anti-return keeper. This distinction must remain essential under an outcome-based score. A new cargo label or extra latch alone is insufficient.
mechanism: Real rail aperture spacing/undercuts, both studs, actual fitting grip and keeper. Unlocked translated fitting must have a real extraction path; engaged keeper must physically prevent it. No magnetic capture or enlarged invented grip.
measurement: Pretrial mark the rail positions; photograph both stud engagement references and visible keeper seating; check hands-clear retention with a disclosed low-load spring-scale test in the applicable directions. The test load/tolerance must be selected after product data; no rated cargo capacity claim. Reject a one-stud hang or supported fitting.
strategy: Bench-mount rail as ordinary cargo hardware, not a cargo-operation scale model. One gripper transports the fitting; the second may hold the actual keeper clear. Align both discs, insert, translate half-pitch per instructions, release keeper and hands. Stock fingertip access is not yet shown.
difficulty: Medium geometry/contact work; low estimated sequence complexity. No measured runtime/action count.
reviews: A—Cargo securement is core; whether installing one anchor alone is consequential enough is threatened by#770. Require a usable restrained tie-down connection outcome, without padding with irrelevant steps.
B—An independent keeper may merely decorate undercut insertion. Read#770/#939 source and the board before asserting novelty.
C—No product-matched dimensional drawing or measured keeper travel is in hand. Do not infer them from a different fitting.
D—Hidden under-lip contact cannot be declared verified by a top photo alone. Provide side access or an unambiguous proof test.
E—A thin release clip may be inaccessible to stock jaws. If it needs a custom enlarged tab, reject this proposed hardware.
F—Likely objection: specialized preparatory anchor step or duplicate rail latch. Resolve importance and topology before assets.

name: SDS-plus full-size chisel exchange
equipment: BoschGBH2-26, fixed SDS-plus tool holder, matching construction chisel; no entire quick-change chuck exchange.
importance: Impact on jobs. Construction laborers use drills/jackhammers as core work; recovered2025 count1,489,300 excludes helpers to avoid double count. Changing work bits during construction setup is more direct than generic maintenance, but its regularity still needs direct procedure/workflow evidence.
comparators: Press and continuously hold release collet while withdrawing pipe; substantial same sleeve-hold/extraction coordination.
Keyed insertion and lug retention; different keyed grooves/ball automatically latch, but connector substitution alone is not new skill.
Two-pin lamp insertion and rotation; shared axial alignment plus constrained rotation and retained endpoint.
distinction: Automatic ball capture into a closed shank groove with keyed open drive grooves, followed by pull-check; removal requires sleeve retract and axial withdrawal. Distinction from the accepted collet release is unresolved and may eliminate it.
mechanism: Stock-size shank with open drive grooves and closed retaining groove, actual chuck guide keys, radial ball and passive sleeve/spring. Preserve axial float of locked SDS shank. Only7mm ball diameter is documented in the recovered parts record; other geometry is not OEM measured.
measurement: Verify correct full-depth lock, allowable axial float, visible sleeve return and failed extraction under a documented modest pull. Do not score zero merely because a locked SDS tool has intended float. After removal, both tool identities and storage locations visible.
strategy: Unpowered/isolated hammer securely mounted as ordinary bench tool servicing; grip actual sleeve and tool at spatially separate sections; retract, withdraw, exchange, rotate during insertion, release/pull-check. Force/reach/contact envelope needs actual hardware data.
difficulty: Medium/high contact-model risk; narrow stock sleeve and key/ball dynamics. Existing draft does not provide native robot success here.
reviews: A—A manual documents how, not how often. #1472 warns that frequent tool use does not automatically make servicing core work. Distinguish recurring work-bit setup from rare repair.
B—#662 already tests holding a release during extraction; keying/ball retention might be only a connector variant, as#766 warns. This is a potentially decisive objection.
C—The actual sleeve/cam and groove profiles must remain; a square groove/pin toy changes the interaction.
D—Locked SDS tools float axially; depth alone cannot measure retention. Calibrate an external pull-and-float observation.
E—No sleeve force curve, stock grasp clearance or full YAM path is verified.
F—Likely objection: duplicate connector exchange or unverified routine core work. Do not implement until these are resolved.

name: Removable scroll-chuck jaw setup and concentric verification
equipment: One identified Röhm geared scroll-chuck family covered byDC0000364 (ZG/ZS/ZGU/ZSU/EG/ES), matching numbered loose jaws and key.
importance: Impact on jobs is unproven. Recovered report sums288,300 machinists+170,000 CNC operators+56,700 tool/die makers=515,000 in2025. Fresh#400 explicitly rejected machinists+tool/die alone below threshold. Adding CNC operators is legitimate only if manual removable-jaw setup is regular core work for that group; no such direct proof was established here.
comparators: Already-assembled jaws clamp a bar and key is removed. Shares chuck/key/workholding outcome; removable tooth-phase acquisition must be the substantive difference.
Four-jaw centering mockup omitted real screws, tightening and runout; warns against loose radial tabs pretending to be a chuck.
Accepted indicator-sweep vise setup: same workholding alignment and independent verification; proposed scroll must add coupled loose-jaw engagement rather than just another alignment target.
distinction: Sequential acquisition of independently loose jaws by one continuous scroll, with tooth-phase errors creating physically eccentric closure. Not “put three numbered objects in slots” or generic bar clamping.
mechanism: Real scroll tooth/jaw pitch, radial guides, engagement depth, stops and key drive. Wrong-phase jaw must physically close at a different radius; no software snap to desired radius.
measurement: After all jaws are engaged, use a specified gauge/mandrel and caliper or indicator inspection for concentric closure and retention. A final gauge test rather than a scored memorized1–2–3 event history permits any physically valid cyclic order. Test load/tolerances await one exact chuck and gauge.
strategy: Chuck anchored with spindle unpowered. One gripper offers a jaw in a guide while the other indexes the scroll with its real key. Verify all teeth engage, then close on gauge and remove key. Free-running torque, jaw mass and key regrasp are unmeasured.
difficulty: High contact fidelity and actuator effort risk; full mechanism requires explicit helical/spiral teeth or a justified causal proxy.
reviews: A—#400 is direct negative evidence: an authentic machining operation can still fail jobs importance. Do not count broader CNC work without proving this actual procedure is core.
B—Starting with jaws removed is not automatically enough differentiation from#400; prove phase acquisition is the central difficulty.
C—Wrong-phase states must be mechanically possible and not corrected by a scripted constraint. Real guides and tooth geometry are required.
D—Arbitrary jaw order is not the outcome; physically concentric retained gauge is. Real runout measurement may require hardware not yet specified.
E—Real chuck key torque and loose-jaw access may exceed stock YAM capability. Do not reduce scale/load to force success.
F—Likely objection: subthreshold specialist work or nonfunctional loose-jaw puzzle. Critical objections unresolved.

name: ER collet-to-nut supported preassembly
equipment: Matched REGO-FIXER32 standard collet/nut family and support fixture that does not invent unsupported retention.
importance: Impact on jobs, conditional. Actual recurring tool-setting procedure, but machinists alone are below500k and #400 prevents casual borrowing of adjacent occupations. A supported collet/nut pair alone may also stop short of a consequential ready toolholder.
comparators: Tilt/align and rotate a captured part under a retaining lip. ER uses an eccentric ring into an annular groove, not bayonet lugs/stops.
Oblique insertion through an insufficient gap, pivot then recenter. Same nonstraight collision path; outcome and interface must be materially distinct.
Accepted machining/plumbing setup where useful outcome is measured after relaxing load; reminds that static tool preparation alone needs an important endpoint.
distinction: Eccentric extraction-ring/groove acquisition by tilt and pivot; straight coaxial push must fail. Avoid claiming a snap ring permanently grips a hanging collet—the manufacturer explicitly warns otherwise.
mechanism: Full-size collet groove/profile and actual eccentric ring offset, matching nut lip, support contacts. No magnets, fake spring detents or captured kinematic attachment.
measurement: Optically inspect visible groove/ring engagement and coaxial assembly on support; a controlled subsequent insertion into the matching holder may provide a useful functional check. A hanging retention test is invalid if the supplier does not guarantee it.
strategy: Two-arm supported manipulation with stock finger contact on appropriate collet lands and nut flats. Lift then tilt/pivot and lower as a supported pair. The preserved full-robot CPU run stalled lifting collet: fix actual grasp before treating waypoint/IK passes as feasibility.
difficulty: High grasp/contact risk despite a short nominal motion sequence. Existing ideal583-action claim is not a complete robot receipt.
reviews: A—Specific setup is authentic; regular-core duty across >500k distinct workers remains unproved. A narrow preparatory step can fail like#770.
B—Collision-constrained oblique insertion exists in#903; a different industrial part is not itself a new capability.
C—Unsupported hang is not guaranteed; do not invent stronger extraction-ring retention.
D—Hidden groove capture needs sight access or a justified functional inspection. No internal coordinate-only score.
E—CPU1263eb9 scored0 after lift stall and speed violation. This is direct unresolved evidence against immediate build-first ranking.
F—Likely objection: insufficient importance/endpoint or duplicated constrained assembly; no green gate at present.

name: RIDGID811A quick-opening die-head setup
equipment: RIDGID811A matched die set, actual head/size bar/washer tongue/clamp; compatible unpowered300Compact fixture.
importance: Impact on jobs, conditional. Historical504,500 plumbers/pipefitters/steamfitters2025 barely exceeds the threshold, but the occupation count does not establish die changes are regular core work for the entire group. Need direct production-threading evidence.
comparators: Tool setup followed by workholding. Shares rotating-key/fixture work; does not acquire four matched cutting dies through a common setting bar.
Place multiple parts in numbered/structured sockets and cap. Die identity/depth must affect functional geometry, not become another count-and-place puzzle.
Pipe joint task has tool engagement and a calibrated useful outcome. A setup-only die task cannot borrow finished-thread quality without a test cut.
distinction: Install four matched numbered dies to physical indicator depth, set shared link index and washer tongue, clamp and prove retention through normal head travel. Distinction is coupled die positioning, not adding more components.
mechanism: Actual die/guide/cam capture, size-bar slot and washer tongue, clamp contact and open/close mechanism. No powered task actuator to seat dies for the robot.
measurement: Physical line flushness, matching die/slot IDs, correct selected size index, tongue seating and retention through normal open/close travel. Does not establish a usable finished thread: manual requires a test cut after changes.
strategy: Unpowered secured head, genuine throwout/clamp controls; open, loosen clamp about three turns, release/reposition washer as instructed, offer dies to correct slots/depth, set index and retighten. No selected control force or gripper access has been verified.
difficulty: Very high geometry/action-count risk; four loose dies and multiple small controls. Powered cutting excluded.
reviews: A—A large plumbing occupation does not make this specialist threading setup routine for all. Need procedure-frequency evidence.
B—Numbered die placement without causal coupled settings degenerates to already-covered assembly.
C—Actual internal cam/guide and tongue interfaces are unavailable dimensionally; do not sketch a new mechanism and call it811A.
D—Manual explicitly requires a test cut. Setup inspection may be a legitimate bounded endpoint, but cannot certify production readiness.
E—Clamp torque, die mass, tool/head envelope and tiny controls may defeat YAM; no reduced-scale workaround is justified.
F—Likely objection: incomplete consequential procedure and unrealistic control access. More risk than first two leads.
